hook.support: You want something to change. A crossing near school. Later buses. A place to skate. Moaning won’t change it. A short, sharp speech to the right people might.
hook.core: You want something to change: a crossing outside school, a later bus, somewhere to skate. Complaining to your mates won’t change it. A short, sharp speech to the people who decide just might. Young people in Victoria and WA have done exactly that.
hook.extend: Most things people want changed never change, because nobody makes the case to the person who can say yes. A short speech with a clear point, solid proof and a specific ask is one of the most powerful tools you have, and young Australians have used it to win crossings, skateparks and more.

why.support: A good speech can change things. It also helps in job interviews, at council and in any group.
why.core: Persuading people is a life skill: asking a boss for more shifts, a council for a crossing, or a group to back your idea. The same simple shape works every time.
why.extend: Persuasion is how decisions get made in workplaces, councils and communities. Knowing how to structure a case, back it with evidence and choose language for a particular audience gives you real influence.

articles.title: Point, proof, punch

body.support:
Want something to change? Make a short speech to the people who can change it.

A strong speech has four parts.

1. **Hook.** Grab them fast. Ask a question. Give a number. Paint a picture.
2. **Point.** Say what you want in **one** sentence.
3. **Proof.** Back it up. Use facts, numbers or a real story. Say where your facts came from.
4. **Punch.** End with a clear ask. Who should do what, and when?

Some word tricks help:

- **Rule of three.** “Safer, quicker, cheaper.”
- **“We” and “you”.** It makes people feel part of it.

Use your own words. Copying someone else’s speech is **plagiarism**. If you use a fact, say where it’s from: “The council website says…”
body.core:
Want something to change? The fastest way is often a short speech to the people who can make it happen. Persuasive speeches that work usually have four parts.

1. **Hook.** Grab attention in the first line: a question (“Who here has nearly been hit crossing Smith Street?”), a striking number, or a picture people can see in their head.
2. **Point.** State what you want in **one clear sentence**. If you can’t say it in one sentence, you’re not ready.
3. **Proof.** Back your point with **evidence**: facts, numbers, an example or a real story. Two or three strong pieces beat ten weak ones. Always say where a fact came from: “According to VicRoads…”. That builds trust, and it avoids **plagiarism**, which is passing off someone else’s words or ideas as your own.
4. **Punch.** End with a **call to action**: who should do what, and by when. “Please put a crossing on Smith Street before next winter.”

Then add some **word power**:

- **Rule of three:** “Safer, quicker, fairer.” Lists of three stick in people’s heads.
- **“We” and “you”:** “We all use this road.” It pulls the audience onto your side.
- **Strong verbs:** “fix”, “build”, “protect”, not “maybe look at”.

Finally, check your script. Clear sentences, paragraphs and correct spelling make you look serious, especially if you send a copy afterwards.
body.extend:
When something needs to change, a short, well-built speech to the people who can make the decision is often more effective than a petition nobody reads. Most persuasive speeches that work follow the same logic.

1. **Hook.** Earn attention in the first line: a direct question, a striking statistic or a vivid image.
2. **Point (contention).** State your position in one precise sentence. Precision matters: “Put a zebra crossing on Thomas Street” is harder to ignore than “Make roads safer”.
3. **Proof.** Support the point with **evidence**: data, examples, expert views or a real story. Choose quality over quantity, and **attribute** every fact (“VicRoads data from 2020 shows…”). Attribution builds credibility and avoids **plagiarism**, which includes paraphrasing someone’s argument without credit.
4. **Punch.** Close with a specific **call to action**: who, what and by when.

Language devices make the logic land:

- **Rule of three:** “Safer, quicker, fairer.”
- **Inclusive language:** “we”, “our town”.
- **Rhetorical questions:** “Do we really want to wait for an accident?”
- **Strong, concrete verbs** and **concrete images** rather than vague abstractions.

Match tone to audience. A council meeting suits formal, respectful language and local evidence; a school assembly can be warmer and more energetic. The structure stays the same; the wording changes.

caseStudies.title: The crossing Flynn talked into existence

body.support:
Flynn lives in Brighton East, in Melbourne. There was no proper crossing on busy Thomas Street. People had to dash across to reach two walking and bike trails.

When Flynn was in primary school, he wrote a letter to the council. He got a reply, but nothing changed.

Years later, at Brighton Secondary College, he entered the **Victoria Parliament Prize**. Students write a speech about a problem in their area.

Flynn called the crossing **“an accident waiting to happen”**. He used proof: about **11,000 vehicles** used that stretch of road. He got his brothers, sisters and neighbours to show how busy it was.

He won. Then the council said it planned to build a crossing.
body.core:
Flynn grew up in Brighton East, in Melbourne. To get between two popular walking and bike trails, people had to cross busy Thomas Street. There was only a small traffic island, no proper crossing.

In primary school, Flynn wrote to the council about it. He got a reply, but nothing happened, and he gave up for a while.

At Brighton Secondary College, he tried again, this time with a speech. He entered the **Victoria Parliament Prize**, where students write a statement about an issue in their community, just like a member of parliament.

His point was clear: Thomas Street needs a crossing. He called it **“an accident waiting to happen”**. His proof included road data: about **11,000 vehicles** used that 1.6-kilometre stretch, according to VicRoads figures from 2020. He even got his siblings and neighbours to help show how busy the road was.

Flynn won the prize. Afterwards, Bayside Council said it planned to put a pedestrian crossing on Thomas Street, once the Department of Transport approved it.
body.extend:
In Brighton East, Melbourne, people walking or riding between two popular trails had to cross Thomas Street, a busy road with only a traffic island. As a primary school student, Flynn wrote to the council asking for a proper crossing. He received a reply but no action.

Years later at Brighton Secondary College, he took another route: the **Victoria Parliament Prize**, in which students write a Member’s Statement about an issue in their community.

His case was tightly built. The point was specific (a crossing on Thomas Street). The hook was memorable (**“an accident waiting to happen”**). The proof was concrete: VicRoads data from 2020 showed about **11,000 vehicles** used the 1.6-kilometre stretch, and he enlisted siblings and neighbours to demonstrate how busy it was.

Flynn won the prize, earning $500 for himself and $1,000 for his school. Bayside Council then said it planned to provide a pedestrian crossing on Thomas Street, pending Department of Transport approval. The same request that stalled as a letter gained momentum as a well-evidenced speech to a bigger audience.

caseStudies.title: A skatepark that started with a speech

body.support:
In 2019, Harry Boylan went to a council meeting in Harvey, a country town in WA. He saw a gap: there was nowhere for young people to skate.

He gave a speech to the council. His friend Jake Baggetta backed him up with a speech too.

The council agreed. In April 2024, the new Harvey skatepark opened.
body.core:
In 2019, Harry Boylan went to a Shire of Harvey council meeting in country Western Australia with an idea. He’d noticed a gap in his town: nowhere decent for young people to skate.

He gave a passionate speech to the councillors, and his friend Jake Baggetta spoke to back him up. The council agreed to the project.

It took time, funding and planning, but the Harvey skatepark officially opened in April 2024. The shire president thanked the town’s young people for pushing for it.
body.extend:
In 2019, Harry Boylan went to a Shire of Harvey council meeting in regional Western Australia. He wanted a skatepark: the town didn’t have one. He spoke to the councillors, and his friend Jake Baggetta gave a speech to back him up.

The council agreed. The project then took nearly five years of planning, design and funding. The skatepark officially opened in April 2024, and the shire president thanked local young people for backing it.

The lesson is about persuasion and persistence. The right audience, a clear proposal and a second voice can start something. Big changes still take time.

model.text:
**To the netball club committee**

Hands up if you’ve waited in the dark for a lift after Tuesday training.

We need the court lights on until 8 pm on training nights.

Right now, they switch off at 7:15. Training finishes at 7:30. Last week I asked 24 players. Nineteen said they had walked to the car park in the dark.

The club’s own safety policy says members must have safe, lit paths to and from the courts.

Longer lights mean safer players, happier parents and fewer worries.

Please vote to change the light timer at next month’s meeting.

teacher.overview: Students learn a four-part persuasive structure (hook, point, proof, punch), collect and attribute evidence, use simple language devices, and deliver a one-minute speech to a real audience. Case studies: Flynn, a Brighton Secondary College student whose Victoria Parliament Prize speech about a crossing led Bayside Council to plan one; and two young locals whose council speeches started the Harvey (WA) skatepark.
prep: Line up real audiences early: principal, SRC, a club committee, or a council youth officer. Even a class acting as “the council” works.
Have devices available for students to find one sourced fact.
Optional: a short clip of a strong youth speech (e.g. a Victoria Parliament Prize entry).

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — The shape of a case
steps: **Hook (10 min):** two versions of the same request: a whinge vs a structured case. Which works?

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Proof
steps: **Case study (15 min):** Flynn. What made the speech stronger than the letter?
**Explicit teaching (10 min):** sources and plagiarism: say where it’s from.
**Get your proof (25 min):** students collect two or three pieces, including one they gather themselves (a count, a quick survey).

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Write it
steps: **Model (10 min):** write the first two lines of a speech aloud.
**Write (30 min):** speeches; peer-check with the checklist.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Make your case
steps: **Speeches (30 min):** to the real or role-played audience.
**Level Up (10 min):** rewrite the punch for a second audience.
**Check & reflect (10 min):** quick check, reflection, sign-off.

keyPoints: Speak to the people who can say yes.

extend: Tone for a named audience; rewrite the punch for two audiences (Level Up).

**Sort:** 31 cars counted — proof; everyone hates — opinion; council website — proof; worst bus route — opinion; 12 students late — proof; I reckon — opinion.

**Annotation:** 1 hook (question); 2 point; 3 proof (own count); 4 proof with source; 5 rule of three; 6 punch / call to action.

realityCheck: **The real audience is what makes this course work.** Book it early. A principal or SRC slot is usually easiest; council youth officers often welcome student speakers.
**Students will want to argue for things they can’t win** (no school, free phones). Steer them to something specific and winnable: that’s the lesson.
**Speaking is frightening for some students.** Offer a smaller audience, a recording, or a written speech sent to the decision-maker (the solo option).
**Proof is the hard part.** Students often have only opinions. The “count it yourself” idea (cars, bikes, a 20-person survey) gets everyone real evidence.
**Works in a real class:** yes, especially when one student’s speech actually gets a result. Share any replies with the class.
